AI generated: In business and economics, the Optimal Stop point (or profit maximization point) occurs when the rate at which you gain (Marginal Revenue) exactly equals the rate at which you spend (Marginal Cost). If the rate of change for your benefit is higher than the rate of change for your cost, you should keep going. Once they flip, you are losing value on every additional unit.

Professor’s Quantitative Breakdown

We are looking for the point where the Marginal Benefit equals the Marginal Cost. This is where your profit "peaks" before diminishing returns make additional hiring a net loss.

Correct Answer: C At 25 workers, your "profit per additional worker" becomes zero. If you hire a 26th worker, the rate of change function R 
′

Visualizing the Profit Peak in R

R
library(ggplot2)

# Define functions
revenue <- function(w) 100 * sqrt(w)
cost <- function(w) 10 * w
profit <- function(w) revenue(w) - cost(w)

# Generate data
w_vals <- seq(1, 50, length.out = 500)
df <- data.frame(
  workers = w_vals,
  revenue = revenue(w_vals),
  cost = cost(w_vals),
  profit = profit(w_vals)
)

# Plotting Profit
ggplot(df, aes(x = workers, y = profit)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkgreen", size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 25, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 28, y = 240, label = "Optimal Stop: 25 Workers", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Total Profit vs. Number of Workers",
       subtitle = "Profit peaks where Marginal Revenue = Marginal Cost",
       x = "Number of Workers (w)",
       y = "Total Profit ($)") +
  theme_minimal()
The "Golden Rule" of Quantitative Reasoning

Always look at the rate of change (the slope) rather than just the total values. The total revenue keeps going up as you hire more people, but the profit eventually goes down because the rate of gain is diminishing while the rate of cost is constant.
